### Original paper

![](media/paper_thumbnail.png)

## Original paper (cont.)

The paper aims to:

- Show that Charikar's SimHash algorithm is effective to generate similar hashes for similar content
- Present an efficient algorithm that allows to detect near-duplicates pairs up to a (reasonably small) factor $K$

In this work only the "batch" version of the proposed algorithm is implemented, using PySpark.

## Types of near-duplicates {.smaller}

Near-duplicates generally fall into two non-exclusive categories:

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Semantic**

*Similar meaning:*

> "a senior couple strolls along the beach while holding hands during sunset"  
> $\approx$  
> "an older couple walks hand in hand on the beach at sunset"
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Syntactic**

*Similar structure:*

> "The quiet librarian suddenly discovered a valuable manuscript inside the forgotten wooden cabinet"  
> $\approx$  
> "The quiet mechanic suddenly discovered a dangerous leak inside the forgotten engine cabinet"
:::

::::

## Potential near-duplicate detection applications {.smaller}

- Remove near-duplicate pages to improve web crawling processes efficiency
- Sanitize datasets from near-duplicate entries
- Spam detection and plagiarism
- Detect malwares from a known dataset of potentially malicious softwares
- Build advanced file systems, able to bundle together files with similar content
- ... and much more!

## Duplicate vs. Near-duplicates

Duplicates are commonly detected using hash functions.

However, hash functions may return vastly different digests for very similar data.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
%%| fig-height: 4
flowchart LR
    subgraph Data
        text1["The quick fox..."]
        text2["The nimble fox..."]
    end
    subgraph Features
        hash1["81223da6..."]
        hash2["7cb0b99c..."]
    end
    text1 -->|hash| hash1
    text2 -->|hash| hash2
```

## Fingerprint generation

A fingerprint is a string of bits of some fixed length that identifies some data.
Fingerprints are generated combining features extracted from data (SimHash algorithm).

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
%%| fig-height: 4
flowchart LR
    data["Data"]
    feature1["Feature"]
    feature2["Feature"]
    feature3["Feature"]
    fingerprint["Fingerprint"]
    data --> feature1 & feature2 & feature3
    feature1 --> fingerprint
    feature2 --> fingerprint
    feature3 --> fingerprint
```

## Feature extraction models

For text data, four different feature models are tested in this work:

1. Bag of words
2. Shingles
3. TF-IDF
4. Embeddings

## Feature Model: Bag of words

Each word in a text is considered a feature.
Easy to compute, but cannot detect locality.
```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
%%| fig-height: 4
flowchart LR
    subgraph Data
        text1["Four plus three"]
    end
    subgraph Words
        word1["Four"]
        word2["plus"]
        word3["three"]
    end
    subgraph Features
        hash1["12f5aedc..."]
        hash2["383ef369..."]
        hash3["8b5b9db0..."]
    end
    text1 --> word1 & word2 & word3
    word1 --> hash1
    word2 --> hash2
    word3 --> hash3
```

## Feature Model: Shingles

A feature is a contiguous series of elements in a text.
Elements can be words or characters, and can be overlapping.
It can generate a large number of features but can detect locality, to some degree.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
%%| fig-height: 4
flowchart LR
    subgraph Data
        text1["Dream"]
    end
    subgraph Shingles ["Shingles over chars, size 3"]
        word1["Dre"]
        word2["rea"]
        word3["eam"]
    end
    subgraph Features
        hash1["9accfb6f..."]
        hash2["c4599aab..."]
        hash3["8fcf84a3..."]
    end
    text1 --> word1 & word2 & word3
    word1 --> hash1
    word2 --> hash2
    word3 --> hash3
```

## Feature Model: TF-IDF {.smaller}

A more sophisticated variant of "Bag of words".
TF-IDF stands for Term Frequency - Inverse Document Frequency.
Each word is weighted for their rarity, inside its text and in the whole dataset.
Rare words have higher weights, while common words have lower weights.
It requires to re-compute all fingerprints when the dataset changes, making it taxing to compute and maintain.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
%%| fig-height: 4
flowchart LR
    subgraph Data
        text1["It's a fork"]
    end
    subgraph Words
        word1["It's"]
        word2["a"]
        word3["fork"]
    end
    subgraph Features ["Features and weights"]
        hash1["1d315be9..., 0.2"]
        hash2["87428fc5..., 0.05"]
        hash3["24ecccc1..., 0.8"]
    end
    text1 --> word1 & word2 & word3
    word1 --> hash1
    word2 --> hash2
    word3 --> hash3
```

## Feature Model: Embeddings

Each text is converted into a set of weights, using the embedding model Qwen3-embedding:0.6b.
The fingerprint is obtained by quantizing each float weight to 0/1, using the median as pivot.
Can require large amount of memory for long inputs.

## Feature models performance {.smaller}

Performed on the *llm-paraphrases* dataset.

TF-IDF is the slowest model: it requires to create a frequency map of all words in the dataset.
Embeddings performance might get worse on datasets with longer texts.

![](media/feature_models_performance.png)

## SimHash

All features of some data are combined by taking the most popular value for each bit index.
This can be sped up using FastSimHash.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
%%| fig-height: 4
flowchart LR
    subgraph Features
        hash1["10010100..."]
        hash2["11010111..."]
        hash3["10101011..."]
    end
    subgraph Fingerprint
        result["10010111..."]
    end
    hash1 --> result
    hash2 --> result
    hash3 --> result
```

## Near-duplicate detection algorithm in PySpark (batch version) {.smaller}

Suppose to have two fingerprint DataFrames, *query* and *dataset* (*query* is always the smaller DataFrame).

1. *query* fingerprints are split into at least $K$ partitions (pigeonhole principle)
2. *query* partitions are collected in a hash table and distributed to all workers, alongside *query* itself
3. Workers iterate over *dataset*, splitting each row into partitions and checking if it matches at least one of the *query* partitions
4. Fingerprint pairs with matching partitions *might* be near-duplicate: if their Hamming distance is less than $K$ they are considered a near-duplicate pair

This algorithm prioritizes locality: only *query* fingerprints and partitions are once sent from the driver to the workers.

## Near-duplicate detection algorithm in PySpark (batch version): schema
<!-- TODO: remake this -->
```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
%%| fig-height: 8
flowchart TD
    subgraph Driver1 ["Driver"]
        query_part_gen["Query partitions generation"]
    end
    subgraph Worker1
        dataset_part_gen1["Dataset partitions generation"]
        part_matching1["Retrieve pairs with matching partitions"]
        candidate_filter1["Filter out pairs with Hamming distance >= K"]
    end
    subgraph Worker2
        dataset_part_gen2["Dataset partitions generation"]
        part_matching2["Retrieve pairs with matching partitions"]
        candidate_filter2["Filter out pairs with Hamming distance >= K"]
    end
    subgraph Driver2 ["Driver"]
        result["All near-duplicate pairs"]
    end
    Query --> Driver1
    query_part_gen --> dataset_part_gen1
    query_part_gen --> dataset_part_gen2
    dataset_part_gen1 --> part_matching1
    part_matching1 --> candidate_filter1
    dataset_part_gen2 --> part_matching2
    part_matching2 --> candidate_filter2
    Worker1 --> Driver2
    Worker2 --> Driver2
```

## ... but why does this work only for small $K$ values? {.smaller}

The graph below shows the expected number of candidates for each query row at different $K$ values.
Higher $K$ values forces the algorithm to adopt small partitions, which generate a large amount of candidates.

![](media/detection_scaling.png)


## Semantic near-duplicates: qqp dataset analysis {.scrollable .smaller}

Sample of 199 rows with 76 near-duplicate rows.

```{python}
#| output: asis
import pandas as pd

def truncate_chars(text, max_chars):
    text = str(text)
    if len(text) > max_chars:
        return text[:max_chars] + "..."
    return text

df = pd.read_csv("media/qqp/qqp_sample.csv")[["data1", "data2", "is_near_duplicate"]]
for col in df.columns:
    df[col] = df[col].apply(lambda x: truncate_chars(x, max_chars=30))

print(df.to_markdown())
```

## Syntax near-duplicates: wikipedia dataset analysis {.scrollable .smaller}

Dataset composed of 1000 wikipedia entries pairs.
Half of them are the same entry but with some random noise (altered words), from 5% to 10%.
The other are pairs of completely different entries.
Due to the large size of each entry, the Embeddings feature model is not considered for this analysis.

```{python}
#| output: asis
import pandas as pd

def truncate_chars(text, max_chars):
    text = str(text)
    if len(text) > max_chars:
        return text[:max_chars] + "..."
    return text

df = pd.read_csv("media/wikipedia/wikipedia_sample.csv")[["data1", "data2", "is_near_duplicate"]]
for col in df.columns:
    df[col] = df[col].apply(lambda x: truncate_chars(x, max_chars=30))

print(df.to_markdown())
```

## Wikipeida: f1score - feature model heatmap

All features models are strong enough to ignore syntactical noise.

![](media/wikipedia/f1score_confusionmatrix.png)

## Real use-case: c5 dataset {.scrollable .smaller}

A fork of the popular c4 dataset, contains Italian web pages content.
This dataset isn't deduplicated.

```{python}
#| output: asis
import pandas as pd

def truncate_chars(text, max_chars):
    text = str(text)
    if len(text) > max_chars:
        return text[:max_chars] + "..."
    return text

df = pd.read_csv("media/c5/c5_sample.csv")[["data"]]
for col in df.columns:
    df[col] = df[col].apply(lambda x: truncate_chars(x, max_chars=75))

print(df.to_markdown())
```

## Improvements over the original paper

- Fingerprints from 32 up to 512 bits (instead of fixed 64 bits)
- $K$ value of any size (instead of $K = 3$)
- Four different feature models available
- Semantic near-duplicate detection
- FastSimHash
